Generate a standardised post-quantum signing key

Source: R/sign.R
fipskg.Rd

Generates a key for one of the NIST-standardised signature schemes: ML-DSA (FIPS 204) or SLH-DSA (FIPS 205). Both are implemented in this package, natively, with no system dependency; pqcbknd() lists the parameter sets. The key signs capsule manifests, attestations and bundles with cpssign(), and its public half, from fipspubkey(), is what you give to anyone who should be able to check those signatures with cpsvrf().

Usage

fipskg(scheme = "ML-DSA-65", seed = NULL)

fipspubkey(key)

Arguments

scheme

Scheme name, one of pqcbknd() other than "xmss-sha256". The default, "ML-DSA-65", is the FIPS 204 middle security level.

seed

Optional raw vector of key-generation seed bytes, of the length fipssz() reports for the scheme. Supplying it makes the key reproducible, which is what the standards' test vectors need; the default draws from the operating system's CSPRNG.

key

A key from fipskg().

Value

fipskg(): a list of class bricklayer_fips_key (also bricklayer_oqs_key) with public and secret (the encoded keys as lowercase hex strings, in the standards' byte layouts) and scheme. Printing it never shows the secret. fipspubkey(): a list of class bricklayer_fips_public_key (also bricklayer_oqs_public_key) with public and scheme.

Details

Unlike pqckg() 's hash-based key, these are STATELESS: one key signs any number of messages, with no index to track and nothing to persist between signatures.

Which to pick. ML-DSA is small and fast and rests on a lattice assumption. SLH-DSA rests on nothing but the hash function, at the cost of a signature one to two orders of magnitude larger; its s parameter sets have small signatures and slow signing, its f sets the reverse, and its SHAKE and SHA-2 families are equally strong: pick SHA-2 where a validated SHA-2 implementation is what an auditor will ask about. "ML-DSA-65" is the sensible default.

Key generation expands a random seed (the length fipssz() reports as seed: 32 bytes for ML-DSA, three times the security level in bytes for SLH-DSA) into the key pair exactly as FIPS 204 ML-DSA.KeyGen and FIPS 205 slh_keygen do, so the same seed gives the same key as any other conforming implementation. ML-DSA keys take milliseconds; SLH-DSA keys take from milliseconds (the f sets) to about a second (the s sets, which build a larger top tree), with a spinner on stderr after 0.75 s when a person is watching (see blprog()) and Ctrl-C honoured. Nothing is written to disk: saving the key, and keeping its secret private, is up to you. fipspubkey() drops the secret half, leaving what a verifier needs.

Refusals: an unknown scheme (the message lists the known ones, and points to pqckg() for XMSS), a seed that is not a raw vector of the right length, and for fipspubkey() a key that did not come from fipskg() or fipskey().

Security

The implementation is hand-written. Its standardised schemes are checked byte for byte against OpenSSL 3.5 and NIST known-answer vectors in the test suite. Side channels are checked, not assumed: inst/ctcheck runs every operation that touches a secret under valgrind memcheck with the secret marked undefined (the ctgrind method), so a branch or a memory address that depends on it is a reported error, and afterwards scans the dead stack for copies of the secret. Both checks run in CI on every change, with GCC and with Clang. Timing is also measured on x86-64 and arm64 hardware (inst/dudect), power leakage is assessed in simulation under the value and the transition models (inst/tvla), and ML-KEM decapsulation and ML-DSA signing are first-order masked by default. These are checks of this code on those compilers and under those leakage models; the README's security section lists what each check does and does not cover.

References

National Institute of Standards and Technology (2024). Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard. FIPS 204. doi:10.6028/NIST.FIPS.204

National Institute of Standards and Technology (2024). Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Standard. FIPS 205. doi:10.6028/NIST.FIPS.205

See also

pqckg() for the stateful hash-based key, cpssign() which accepts either, fipssz() for the byte lengths.

Examples

key <- fipskg("ML-DSA-65")
key$scheme
#> [1] "ML-DSA-65"

sig <- cpssign("a manifest digest", key)
cpsvrf("a manifest digest", sig, fipspubkey(key))
#> [1] TRUE

# A context string binds the signature to its purpose: the same
# message signed for one context does not verify under another.
sig2 <- cpssign("a manifest digest", key, ctx = "release")
cpsvrf("a manifest digest", sig2, key, ctx = "release")
#> [1] TRUE
cpsvrf("a manifest digest", sig2, key, ctx = "staging")
#> [1] FALSE

# A fixed seed reproduces the key (for test vectors only: a guessable
# seed is a guessable key).
seed <- as.raw(1:32)
identical(fipskg("ML-DSA-44", seed)$public, fipskg("ML-DSA-44", seed)$public)
#> [1] TRUE

# The public half carries no secret.
names(fipspubkey(key))
#> [1] "public" "scheme"

# An unknown parameter set is refused.
try(fipskg("ML-DSA-99"))
#> Error : unknown scheme 'ML-DSA-99'. The standardised schemes are: ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, ML-DSA-87, SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s, SLH-DSA-SHA2-128f, SLH-DSA-SHA2-192s, SLH-DSA-SHA2-192f, SLH-DSA-SHA2-256s, SLH-DSA-SHA2-256f, SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s, SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128f, SLH-DSA-SHAKE-192s, SLH-DSA-SHAKE-192f, SLH-DSA-SHAKE-256s, SLH-DSA-SHAKE-256f. For the stateful hash-based scheme use pqckg().
